rows.label: Concept
rows.text: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity vector rotates, so an acceleration must act: **centripetal acceleration** $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$, always directed to the centre. The derivation (NEB 2023, 2024, 5m) uses the similarity between the velocity triangle and the position triangle: $\Delta v/v = v\Delta t/r$, hence $a_c = v^2/r$.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - a_c = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T² - F_c = mv²/r = mω²r

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Inertial/Non-Inertial Distinction:** Centripetal force is a real resultant force in an inertial frame; it is not a 'fictitious' force. Fictitious centrifugal force only appears in the rotating reference frame to maintain Newton's laws.  ·  **Directional Constraint:** Centripetal force must act strictly perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity for the speed to remain constant. If the net force has a tangential component, the speed changes (non-uniform circular motion).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Always identify which real force provides the centripetal force — never add 'centripetal force' as a separate force in the FBD.  ·  Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force — it appears only in rotating reference frames, not in inertial frames.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Stone on string*** — 0.5 kg at 4 m/s on 1 m: T = 8 N supplies F_c.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Centripetal vs centrifugal:** only the inward force is real; centrifugal is a rotating-frame illusion.  ·  **$F_c$ is not a new force:** it is whichever real force (tension, gravity, friction) points inward.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 problems calculating centripetal force/acceleration for different scenarios.  ·  Solve 5 maximum-speed problems (string breaking, car skidding) using F_c = mv²/r.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Write the definition with direction — it carries marks."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Derivation (5m): Derive a_c = v²/r for uniform circular motion.** — Particle moves A→B in time Δt sweeping Δθ; velocity rotates by the same Δθ. Chord AB = vΔt ≈ rΔθ. The velocity triangle (v, v, Δv) is similar to the position triangle (r, r, AB): Δv/v = AB/r = vΔt/r. So Δv/Δt = v²/r; as Δt→0, a_c = v²/r, directed towards the centre.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The derivation appeared in two consecutive years (2023, 2024) — learn it with the diagram.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The 5m derivation:** velocity triangle similar to position triangle → Δv/v = vΔt/r → a_c = v²/r (NEB 2023, 2024).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$, directed to the centre; $F_c = mv^2/r = m\omega^2 r$.  ·  Uniform circular motion: speed constant, velocity direction changing, net force inward.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Satellites are in free fall — gravity is their centripetal force; no engine holds them up.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A 1000 kg car turns a flat curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. The minimum coefficient of friction to prevent skidding is: (g = 10 m/s²) → C  ·  A 0.5 kg ball on a 1.5 m string rotates at 4 m/s. The tension is: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Force That Bends Motion Uniform circular motion needs an acceleration even though the speed never changes — because the *direction* of velocity changes every instant. That inward acceleration, and the force behind it, governs every turning car, whirling stone and orbiting satellite.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2023, 2024) ### 2.1 Definition **Centripetal acceleration** is the acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion, directed along the radius **towards the centre**, of magnitude $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$. **Centripetal force** is the net force producing it: $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 23:** $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$ — the two forms. - **To Topic 26/27:** at the top of a vertical circle and on banked roads, gravity/friction/normal supply $F_c$. - **To Newton's second law:** $F_c = ma_c$ is just $F = ma$ applied along the radius.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Radius Variation:** If the path radius $r$ changes during the motion, the centripetal force requirement $F_c = mv^2/r$ must adjust instantaneously based on the new radius and speed at that instant.  ·  If the centripetal force is removed, the body moves tangent to the circle (Newton's first law).  ·  Maximum-speed problems: set F_c = mv²/r equal to the maximum available force (tension, friction) and solve for v.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB frequently asks: 'Find the maximum speed' — use v_max = √(μ_s rg) for curves, v_max = √(T_max r/m) for strings.  ·  Verified PYQs: derivation (2023, 2024 — 5m each); car-turn numerical (2022, 2024 — 3m).  ·  "Centripetal force always acts towards the centre along the radius."

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: What supplies the centripetal force for a car turning on a flat road?  ·  Solve 3 problems identifying which real force provides the centripetal force.  ·  Solve 3 problems linking linear and angular quantities (a_c = rω²).
